description:
We are Project Prometheus, a team from Thessaloniki taking on the challenge “Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions”. Like Prometheus, who brought fire to humanity, we want to bring data and technology to protect those who explore the unknown.

Our idea is to combine sensors/hardware with software that tracks astronauts’ vital signs in real time, analyzes the data, and flags early warning signs, with a clear dashboard for both crew and mission control.
summary:
Crew Readiness Check is a 3-minute daily readiness practice for astronauts, run by simple software. Each morning the astronaut takes a 3-minute reaction-time test and rates their sleepiness from 1 to 9, and the app adds last night's sleep from a wrist activity tracker. Results are compared with the astronaut's own baseline, recorded on Earth before flight and re-checked early in the mission, and shown as green, yellow or red with a clear next step. The commander sees only "available" or "not now", so personal data stays private.

It combines three methods already proven on Earth: the Psychomotor Vigilance Test (used on the ISS, in aviation and in trucking), personal fatigue modelling from US Army research, and the decision rules of fatigue risk management in aviation and trucking.

Why it matters: ISS astronauts slept about 6 hours a night on average, below the 7-hour minimum recommended for adults, and tired people often miss their own decline. On the way to Mars, an answer from Earth can take up to 44 minutes. Our prototype (synthetic data) lets the crew check readiness on board in 3 minutes, not 44.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS
Crew Readiness Check answers one question before the work day and before any critical task, such as a spacewalk: is this astronaut rested enough right now? It takes about 3 minutes and has three inputs:
- Test: a 3-minute reaction-time test (PVT-B), the same type as NASA's Reaction Self Test, used on the ISS since 2009.
- Feel: a sleepiness rating from 1 to 9 (Karolinska Sleepiness Scale).
- Sleep: last night's sleep from a wrist activity tracker (actigraph), the same type of device NASA flew on Artemis II. Actigraphs tend to overestimate sleep, so we subtract an illustrative 30-minute margin and never decide on sleep alone.

The results are compared with the astronaut's own baseline, in two layers: one recorded on Earth before flight, and a re-baseline in the first days of the mission, because reaction times can change in space. General limits, such as less than 7 hours of sleep, stay as a safety net.

The astronaut sees green (ready), yellow (caution) or red (not now), with a short "why" and a clear next step: for example, take a nap, wait 20 minutes and test again, or hand the task to a rested crewmate. A mismatch alert ("you feel fine, but your reactions say otherwise") catches the most dangerous case, because people's sense of sleepiness levels off while their performance keeps falling. The escalation path is: astronaut, then Crew Medical Officer, then commander, then flight surgeons on Earth when the link allows. The commander sees only "available" or "not now" for each crew member, never the personal data.

Our prototype shows four screens: the morning check, the colour result with guidance, the commander view for a crew of 4, and the message to Earth with the expected reply time. Demo scenario: Astronaut 4 sleeps short for three nights, goes from yellow to red, and the spacewalk goes to a rested crewmate. All data is synthetic and all thresholds are illustrative.

BENEFITS
- Objective: the 3-minute test shows no practice effect, and every attempt is saved, so it is hard to "beat".
- Cheap in crew time: about 3 minutes, no training needed.
- No new hardware: a tablet and a wrist actigraph, both already flown.
- Private by design, and it works on board without waiting for Earth.

INTENDED IMPACT
Goal: no tired astronaut starts a critical task. There have been 286 spacewalks at the ISS since 1998, and each one needs a ready crew. On the way to Mars, an answer from Earth can take up to 44 minutes, and NASA plans to move more medical decisions on board (Earth-Independent Medical Operations). We do not claim a percentage reduction in errors, because there are no published counts of fatigue-caused errors in space. Instead, we would measure three things in an analog habitat such as NASA HERA: the share of critical tasks started in green, the "feels fine, tests worse" cases caught, and the minutes from test to decision. On Earth, the same low-cost, offline routine could help small isolated teams without fatigue support, such as Antarctic stations, small ships and expeditions (a hypothesis to test). This is the first module of a full crew health monitor; heart rate, blood pressure and temperature come next.

TOOLS WE USED
- Prototype: [TEAM TO FILL: languages, frameworks, tools, hosting]
- Pitch deck: Microsoft PowerPoint
- Research: NASA Human Research Program pages, NASA Technical Reports Server, Canadian Space Agency pages and peer-reviewed studies (see References)
- AI: Claude (Anthropic) for research support, fact-checking and drafting the deck (see the AI section)

HOW IT IS CREATIVE
We did not invent a new device or test. We took three practices already proven on Earth (the Psychomotor Vigilance Test from aviation and trucking, personal fatigue modelling from US Army research, and the fatigue risk management rules of airlines and truck fleets) and combined them into one 3-minute routine for space. Today, fatigue on the ISS is managed with support from the ground; our routine moves that decision on board. In the published tools we reviewed, we found no alert that compares how tired you feel with how you actually perform.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED
- Crew time: under 5 minutes, like NASA's own design rule for the Reaction Self Test.
- Honesty: astronauts may hide fatigue to keep a task, so the commander sees only availability, data is not used for future crew selection, and any points reward consistency, not "green".
- Space changes what "normal" means, hence the in-flight re-baseline.
- Communication delays and blackouts, hence decisions on board.
